1 Solid-state synthesis of Cu nanoparticles embedded in carbon substrate for efficient electrochemical reduction of carbon dioxide to formic acid Fangqi Yang,a Chang Jiang,a Mingfeng Ma,a Fenghao Shu,a Xinyu Mao,a Weikang Yu,a Jun Wang,a* Zheling Zeng,a Shuguang Deng b* a School of Resource, Environmental and Chemical Engineering, Nanchang University, No. 999 Xuefu Avenue, Jiangxi 330031, RP China b School for Engineering of Matter, Transport and Energy, Arizona State University, 551 E. Tyler Mall, Tempe, AZ 85287, USA *Corresponding author: E-mail: jwang7@ncu.edu.cn (J. Wang) E-mail: shuguang.deng@asu.edu (S. Deng)
2 Abstract ： Electrochemical reduction of CO2 into formic acid (HCOOH) is an appealing approach to mitigate the CO2 emission problem and achieve a carbon-neutral cycle but remains a challenge. Herein, we present a novel strategy to prepare Cu nanoparticles embedded in carbon substrate (Cu NPs@C) as efficient CO2 reduction reaction electrocatalysts for highly selective HCOOH production. The uniformly distributed Cu nanoparticles are responsible for the high faradaic efficiency of HCOOH of 78% at -1.0 V (RHE) and yield of 82.8 μmol h-1 cm-2 at -1.2 V (RHE). Moreover, the detailed density functional theory (DFT) calculations have demonstrated that the high activity and selectivity for HCOOH production was attributed to the synergy effects of exposed Cu (111) facets and carbon substrate. The charges transferred from Cu induces a charge-rich environment on the carbon surface, which enhances the *OCHO adsorption and boosts the HCOOH formation. This work paves a new way to synthesize novel Cu-based electrocatalysts for efficient production of HCOOH. Keywords: CO2 electrochemical reduction; mechanical ball-milling; Cu-based electrocatalyst; HCOOH production; DFT calculation
3 Introduction. The excessive use of fossil fuels leads to the ever-growing carbon dioxide (CO2) concentration in the atmosphere. Effective approaches that can achieve a carbon-neutral cycle are urgently desired to alleviate global warming and abnormal climate problems.1 Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), combined with the utilization of renewable and intermittent electricity, could efficiently convert CO2 into valuable chemical feedstocks or carbon-neutral fuels in mild reaction conditions.2 However, CO2 molecules are thermodynamically inert with a stable C=O bond (~806 kJ mol-1), and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) makes it very challenging to simultaneously obtain a desirable product with high selectivity and activity.3,4 Through the rational design of electrocatalysts, a wide range of reduced products could be obtained under different overpotentials, including carbon monoxide (CO), formic acid (HCOOH), methane (CH4), ethanol (C2H6O), ethylene (C2H4), and isopropanol (C3H8O).4,5 The 2-electron reduction pathways to produce CO and HCOOH are highly promising owing to their high selectivities and large partial current densities.4 The effective production of HCOOH is highly desirable due to its nature of multipurpose liquid fuel with high energy density and easy to transport. Meanwhile, HCOOH could serve as a facile H2 source that the same volume of HCOOH can provide 580-fold more H2 compared to that of pure gaseous H2 for fuel cell applications.6,7 However, developing novel electrocatalysts with high HCOOH faradaic efficiency (FE), product selectivity, and partial current density are still very challenging.8,9 Metal-based electrocatalysts have been intensively investigated in terms of
4 theoretical calculation and experimental evaluation as the most effective materials for CO2 reduction to HCOOH, such as Sn,8,10 Pb,11 In,12 and Cu.5,9,13 However, the elaborate modulations of particle size, morphology, and grain boundary of metal nanoparticles/alloys are inevitable, which severely hindered their large-scale applications.4,14 Recently, the non-noble Cu-based electrocatalysts have attracted wide attention due to their natural abundance and diverse reduction products ranging from C1 to C2+.9,15 Whereas, the relatively poor product selectivity causes the tedious separation processes in subsequent applications. Although various design and synthesis strategies have been attempted on Cu-based catalysts, the FE on HCOOH is still disappointing, yet rarely exceeds 40% on Cu-based catalysts.2,5,16 Previous studies have shown that the surface orientation plays a vital role in determining the selectivity of CO2RR products on Cu-based catalyst, because the binding energies of intermediates (*COOH, *CO, *OCHO, *OCH3, etc.) vary significantly on different crystal facets.1719 For example, Sen et al. systematically investigated the Cu (111), (100), and (211) surfaces on CO2RR, and revealed that the (211) surface was the most active for hydrocarbon production, owing to the stronger binding energy of *CO intermediate.15 Cao and co-workers comparatively studied the reaction pathways on different Cu facets by performing density functional theory (DFT) calculations and disclosed that the open and metastable facets, such as (110) and reconstructed (110), were responsible for CO production.18 Meanwhile, the Cu (111) facet showed improved catalytic activity for HCOOH production at low overpotentials owing to the moderate binding energy of *OCHO was also reported.17 Thus, full exposure of Cu (111) facet is proposed as an
5 effective way to selectively reduce CO2 to HCOOH. It should be noted that, besides the intrinsic property of the active sites, carbon substrates (like graphene, carbon black, and carbon nanotube) have been designed and demonstrated to successfully disperse and stabilize the metal nanoparticles (NPs), and further avert the self-agglomeration, oxidation, and deactivation of active sites.10,21 Moreover, the carbon substrates with high surface area and hierarchical pore structure can facilitate the mass transfer and enhance the CO2 adsorption, and further forming a high CO2-concentration local microenvironment around the solid/liquid/gas tripleinterface.10 However, the conventional wet-chemistry approaches for preparing carbonsupported metal NPs always require poisonous organic solvents and strict reaction conditions.10,20,21 Thus, facile and green assembling of metal NPs and carbon substrates under mild conditions is urgent but challenging. Because carbon substrates tend to corrode the metal surface in the catalytic process, and always, the weak interactions between the carbon substrates and metal NPs lead to the leaching and aggregation of metal NPs.22,23 Herein, we report a facile and green mechanical ball-milling approach to prepare uniformly distributed Cu nanoparticles embedded in carbon substrate (Cu NPs@C) with a maximum exposure of Cu (111) facet. By virtue of the optimized surface orientation and rational structure design, the obtained Cu NPs@C can exclusively convert CO2 into HCOOH with an excellent FE of 78% and a selectivity of 87.6% at - 1.0 V (vs. RHE), as well as the long-term catalytic stability of 24 h. Furthermore,
6 density functional theory (DFT) calculations suggested that the optimal Cu (111) facet together with the carbon substrate facilitates the charge transfer and promotes the key *OCHO intermediate formation in HCOOH evolution. This work provides a novel ballmilling approach to prepare efficient and HCOOH-selective CO2RR catalysts as well as new insights into their structure-function relationships.

sections.heading: Experimental section
sections.text:
Material. All chemical reagents were used as received without further purification. Copper (II) acetate monohydrate (Cu(OAc)2·H2O), Pluronic F-127, tannin acid, and potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3) were purchased from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd. Ethanol was obtained from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd. Ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ) was supplied by a UP water purification system. Nafion solution (5 wt%) and carbon paper (HCP 030) were acquired from Sigma-Aldrich and Shanghai Hesen Electric Co., Ltd, respectively. Carbon dioxide (99.999%) and nitrogen (99.999%) were purchased from Nanchang Guoteng Gas Co., Ltd. Catalyst preparation. In a typical synthesis, tannin acid (1.0 g) and Pluronic F-127 (1.0 g) were added to an agate jar (50 ml) with 10 grinding beads (4 × diameter 1.2 cm and 6 × diameter 0.6 cm). The jar was placed in a planetary ball mill (QM-3SP04) with the rotating speed of 360 rounds min-1. After milling for 30 min, a certain amount of Cu(OAc)2·H2O was added to the jar and milled for another 30 min. The obtained gellike mixture was washed thoroughly with ethanol and ultrapure water, followed by vacuum drying at 60 ℃ overnight. Then, the products were carbonized in a tube furnace
7 at 600 ℃ for 2 h with a heating rate of 5 ℃ min-1 under N2 atmosphere. The samples with 1, 3, and 5 mmol Cu(OAc)2·H2O loading were denoted as Cu NPs-1@C, Cu NPs3@C, and Cu NPs-5@C, respectively. Electrochemical tests. All electrochemical measurements were conducted on an electrochemical workstation (CHI 630E). A Pt foil (2 × 2 cm) and saturated Ag/AgCl were utilized as the counter and reference electrode, respectively. All potentials were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) using the formula of E (V vs. RHE) = E (V vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 V + 0.0591 × pH. The working electrode was prepared by mixing active material (10 mg), carbon black (10 mg), 5 % Nafion solution (100 μL), and ethanol (1 mL) under sonication for 2 h and painted homogeneously (100 μL) onto a carbon paper (1 × 1 cm2) as with a catalyst loading mass about 1 mg cm-2. The CO2RR experiments were performed on a two-compartment electrochemical cell at ambient conditions and separated by an anion exchange membrane (Nafion®, 212) to avoid the oxidation of CO2 reduction products. Each chamber contained 20 mL 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte and 30 mL headspace. Before each electrolysis test, the cathodic electrolyte was saturated by bubbling CO2 gas for at least 30 min (pH = 6.8). During the reaction, CO2 gas was continuously purged at a flow rate of 20 mL min-1. The gas products were delivered into online gas chromatography (GC, Agilent 7890 B), and H2 and CO were analyzed by a Haysep Q column packed TCD detector, hydrocarbons were surveyed by an Alumina column packed FID detector. The catholyte after electrolysis was collected and quantified via 1H nuclear magnetic resonance
8 spectroscopy (NMR, Bruker, Avance 400) with a water suppression method.

sections.heading: Results and discussion
sections.text:
Structure characterizations. The facile ball-milling synthesis approach is illustrated in Figure 1a. Primarily, the carbon substrate was fabricated by the self-assemble of tannin acid (carbon precursor) and amphiphilic surfactant of F-127 (soft template). The intrinsic catechol- and pyrogallol-like radicals in tannin acid are capable of integrating with F-127 through the hydrogen- and coordination-interactions to form a rigid network.25,26 After ball-milling for 30 min, copper acetate was added into the mixture for another 30 min of ball-milling. Interestingly, besides the role of providing Cu sources into the carbon support, the copper acetate was able to enhance the crosslinking degree and facilitate the self-assembly of tannin acid around F-127 micelles. It could be confirmed by the controlled experiment (without copper acetate) that no solid sample was obtained after ethanol washing. Finally, the composite was calcinated in an N2 atmosphere, where F-127 micelles were completely decomposed and volatilized. Meanwhile, Cu species were reduced to metallic Cu nanoparticles. The detailed sample morphologies with different Cu doping contents are given in Figure S1a-c. The threedimensional (3D) Cu NPs@C monoliths possess a similar bulky morphology with a rough surface. The TEM images depicted that the Cu nanoparticles were embedded in the carbon substrate with an average diameter of about 0.24 μm (Figures 1b,c and S2). A high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) image of Cu NPs-3@C disclosed a clear boundary of Cu nanoparticle and carbon substrate, and the lattice fringe spacing was measured to
9
be 0.22 nm that belongs to the d (111) crystal plane of metallic Cu (Figure 1d).27 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX), further verified the homogeneous dispersion of Cu nanoparticles over the entire carbon substrate (Figure 1e).
Figure 1. Schematic illustration of the fabrication process of Cu NPs@C (a); TEM image (b and c); HR-TEM image (d), and corresponding EDX mapping image (e) of Cu NPs-3@C.
The existence of metallic Cu nanoparticles embedded in the carbon substrate was further identified by the XRD and XPS characterizations. As shown in Figure 2a, the
10
XRD patterns of Cu NPs@C showed three obvious diffraction peaks at 2θ = 43.3°, 50.4°, and 74.2° that could be assigned to the (111), (200), and (220) planes of metallic Cu (JCPDS: 85-1326), respectively.17 While the high-resolution XPS Cu 2p spectra (Figure 2b) displayed two peaks located at 932.5 and 952.4 eV, corresponding to the Cu 2p3/2 and Cu 2p1/2 state of metallic Cu0 state, respectively.5,17 The formation of metallic Cu nanoparticles is likely ascribed to the reduction of Cu2+ species by the adjacent carbons in the inert atmosphere during thermal treatment.28 Raman spectra of the obtained Cu NPs@C were applied to further study the local disorder and crystallinity. Figure 2c showed two characteristic bands that appeared at 1350 and 1580 cm-1, which correspond to the D- and G-band of the carbon substrate, respectively.29 The D-band features the disorder-induced defects, while the G-band implies the inplane vibration of sp2-hybridized carbon in the graphite layers. The intensity ratio of Dand G-bands (ID/IG) quantified the defect concentration,30 where the ID/IG ratios of Cu NPs-1@C, Cu NPs-3@C, and Cu NPs-5@C were calculated to be 1.01, 0.91, and 0.88, respectively, implying that the Cu nanoparticles were able to facilitate the formation of ordered graphic structures. The accurate Cu mass loading of 8.42, 17.75, and 29.29 wt.% was determined on Cu NPs-1@C, Cu NPs-3@C, and Cu NPs-5@C by ICP-OES, respectively. The specific Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface areas were investigated by the N2 adsorption/desorption isotherms at 77 K (Figure 2d), which displayed the characteristic features of type IV isotherms with a hysteresis loop at high relative pressure regions according to the IUPAC classification, indicating the hierarchical pore systems of micro/mesopores.31,32 The BET specific surface areas were
11
evaluated to be 328, 256, and 144 m2 g-1 on Cu NPs-1@C, Cu NPs-3@C, and Cu NPs5@C, respectively. The pore size distribution curves in Figure S3 displayed two main peaks centered at about 1.38 and 1.69 nm. The obtained hierarchical pore systems could facilitate the electrolyte filtration and CO2 transfer and further boost the CO2RR performances.33
Electrochemical characterization. The electrocatalytic CO2 reduction performances on Cu NPs@C were evaluated in a typical three-electrode system with CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous electrolyte. The linear sweep voltammogram (LSV) curves in N2- or CO2-saturated electrolyte were conducted to evaluate the catalytic activity
12
toward CO2RR in a potential range of 0 ~ -1.2 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) at a scan rate of 10 mV s-1. The potentials are all referred to RHE afterward. As shown in Figure 3a, The occurrences of CO2RR were illustrated by the significantly higher current densities (j) in the CO2-saturated electrolyte than that of N2saturated electrolyte. Specifically, the CO2RR onset potential of -0.47 V was recorded on Cu NPs-3@C that is more positive than that of Cu NPs-1@C (-0.62 V) and Cu NPs5@C (-0.55 V). Moreover, Cu NPs-3@C achieved a high current density of -8.69 mA cm-2 at -1.2 V, whereas, only -3.21 and -5.57 mA cm-2 were recorded on Cu NPs-1@C and Cu NPs-5@C at the same potential. These results strongly indicate that the superior catalytic activity on Cu NPs-3@C. The gaseous and liquid products of CO2RR at -0.8 to -1.2 V were detected by gas chromatography (GC) and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, respectively. The total product FEs of HCOOH (FEHCOOH), CO (FECO), and H2 (FEH2) on three samples are close to 100% (Figures 3b-d). As expected, Cu NPs-3@C exhibited a superior CO2RR activity and the highest FE of CO2RR products (FEC-products) that combines FEHCOOH and FECO over the whole potential range (Figure S4). At the potential of -1.0 V, the maximum FEC-products of 89% was achieved on Cu NPs-3@C with the highest FEHCOOH of 78%, yielding the selectivity of 87.6% (Figure 3c). This result is superior or competitive to many toplevel Cu-based catalysts, as listed in Table S4. At more negative potentials, the FECproducts declined gradually due to the mass diffusion-limitation under large overpotentials.17 As for Cu NPs-1@C, HCOOH is the exclusive product, but with a lower FEHCOOH of 51% at -1.0 V (Figure 3b). Cu NPs-5@C displayed the highest
13
FEHCOOH of 53% at -0.9 V with a selectivity of 87.4% (Figure 3d).
Figure 3. LSV curves in N2- (dashed line) and CO2- (solid line) saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte at a scan rate of 10 mV s-1 (a); FE for all products and HCOOH selectivity versus applied potentials of Cu NPs-1@C (b), Cu NPs-3@C (c), Cu NPs-5@C (d).
Moreover, the production rates of HCOOH on Cu NPs-3@C were significantly faster than that of Cu NPs-1@C and Cu NPs-5@C over the whole potential range from -0.8 to -1.2 V (Figure 4a). The HCOOH production rate on Cu NPs-3@C gradually increased from 38.0 μmol h-1 cm-2 at -0.8 V to 82.8 μmol h-1 cm-2 at -1.2 V, which is 3.1 and 1.8 times higher than that of Cu NPs-1@C and Cu NPs-5@C, respectively. The energy efficiencies (EEs) were also estimated to assess the overall energy utilization efficiency in the CO2RR process.19 As shown in Figure 4b, Cu NPs-3@C exhibited the maximum EE value of 50.1% at -1.0 V. In contrast, Cu NPs-1@C and Cu NPs-5@C
14
only reached a moderate EE of 32.2% and 36.4%, respectively. To confirm the origin of HCOOH is CO2 rather than the carbon substrate or HCO3- ions in KHCO3 electrolyte, the 13CO2 labeling experiments were conducted and the products were analyzed by the 1H and 13C NMR (Figure S7). The signal at 164.5 ppm was observed in the 13C NMR spectrum, which could be ascribed to H13COO- ions. Furthermore, the proton-coupled 1H NMR doublet of 13C in H13COO- ions also appeared at 8.5 ppm. These observations confirm that the HCOOH is the product of CO2RR.34
The electrochemical active areas (ESCA) were measured by the double-layer capacitances to determine the accessible electroactive sites (Figures 4c and S9).5,35 Notably, Cu NPs-3@C showed the highest electrochemical double-layer capacitance of 33 mF cm-2 than Cu NPs-1@C (12 mF cm-2) and Cu NPs-5@C (6 mF cm-2). Furthermore, the adsorption affinities between the catalyst surface and CO2 molecules were demonstrated by the isosteric heats of adsorption (Qst) that calculated from the Clausius-Clapeyron equation based on the CO2 adsorption isotherms at 273, 298, and 323 K. As given in Figure S10, the obtained Cu NPs@C exhibited the enhanced CO2 uptake capacities in the range of 1.12 (Cu NPs-1@C) ~ 1.35 mmol g-1 (Cu NPs-3@C) at 298 K thanks to the high specific surface areas. The highest initial Qst of 41.8 kJ mol-1 was also obtained on Cu NPs-3@C, which is higher than that of Cu NPs-1@C (40.3 kJ mol-1) and Cu NPs-5@C (37.4 kJ mol-1), as shown in Figure S10d. The stronger interaction force on Cu NPs-3@C coupled with the high CO2 uptake capacity lead to the high CO2 concentration around the active sites to compensate for the limited CO2
15
solubility at aqueous electrolyte.34 The excellent stability was further demonstrated by the continuous electrolysis experiment for 24 h on Cu NPs-3@C. The current density and the FEHCOOH almost keep intact at -5.26 mA cm-2 and 78%, respectively (Figure 4d). The XRD patterns of Cu NPs-3@C after a prolonged electrocatalysis process also confirmed its structure stability (Figure S11).

The effects of electrolyte concentration were further investigated, the HCO3- ions
not only act as a proton donor but also ensure the supply of CO2 via rapid equilibrium with bicarbonate.33 When the concentration of KHCO3 solution increased from 0.1 to 0.5 M, the overall current densities increased from -5.8 to -11.3 mA cm-2, whereas,
16
FEHCOOH decreased from 78% to 57% at -1.0 V on Cu NPs-3@C (Figure S12a). The relationship between HCOOH partial current density and KHCO3 concentration was plotted in Figure S12b, the slope of 0.23 demonstrated that the influence of HCO3concentration is negligible on the CO2 reduction8,36 Furthermore, the CO2RR activities under different CO2 flow rates were examined on Cu NPs-3@C in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (Figure S13). The overall current densities increased with CO2 flow rate increasing from 5 to 20 mL min-1, the corresponding FEs and yield rates of HCOOH also changed consistently. This can be ascribed to the promoted mass transfer on the porous structure of carbon substrates.37 When flow rates further increased to 30 and 40 mL min-1, the current density, FEs, and yield rates of HCOOH slightly decreased, implying that the mass transfer had reached its limit caused by the relatively slow desorption of HCOOH.2
DFT calculations. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to elucidate the CO2RR reaction mechanisms. Since three facets of Cu (111), (200), and (220) were observed on Cu NPs@C, the Gibbs free energies of key intermediates on different facets are estimated. As displayed in Figure 5a, despite the *OCHO intermediates are strongly adsorbed on Cu (200) and (220) facets than Cu (111) facet, the releases of *OCHO to produce HCOOH are obviously energy unfavorable with a large uphill free energy of 1.14 and 1.42 eV on (200) and (220) facets, respectively. Comparatively, Cu (111) facet possesses a moderate *OCHO binding energy of 0.42 eV and facile release energy of 0.03 eV. Given that the Cu (111) facet was largely
17
exposed and the most favorable reaction sites (Table S2), the Cu (111) facet is identified as the catalytic active sites for the preferential HCOOH production. In order to illustrate the origin of high HCOOH selectivity, we also calculated the required free energies for CO and H2 generation. As for CO production (Figure 5b), the formation energy of key intermediate (*COOH) was determined to be 1.28 eV on Cu (111) facet that is much higher than those of 0.97 eV on (200) facet and 0.76 eV on (220) facet, suggesting its poor electrochemical ability for CO generation. Notably, the Gibbs free energy for *COOH formation (1.28 eV) was also much higher than that of *OCHO (0.42 eV), thus HCOOH was the preferred product and the CO production was strongly inhibited on Cu (111) facet. These results also explained the absence of hydrocarbon products on obtained Cu NPs@C catalysts, due to the limited production of *CO intermediate.14,35 Moreover, the hydrogen evolution reaction was also inhibited on Cu (111) facet as demonstrated by the higher energy barrier of 0.36 eV of *H adsorption than that of (200) facet (0.33 eV) and (220) facet (0.27 eV), as shown in Figure 5c.
To evaluate the essential role of carbon substrate, DFT calculations were further
carried out on a coordination system of the Cu (111)@C structure (Figure S14), as Figure 5d depicted that the adsorption energy of *OCHO intermediates significantly enhanced with the presence of carbon substrate. Specifically, the endothermic adsorption on Cu (111) facet has changed to the favorable exothermic adsorption on Cu (111)@C system, as the corresponding free energy decreases from 0.42 to -0.35 eV. Moreover, the rate-determining step (RDS) has altered from the CO2→*OCHO step
18
with a barrier energy of 0.42 eV on Cu(111) facet to the *OCHO→HCOOH step with a barrier energy of 0.36 eV on Cu (111)@C system. Thus, the carbon layer can decrease the energy barriers to steer the CO2RR activity. The charge transfer and electron redistribution on the Cu (111)@C system are proposed to induce performance enhancement. The charge difference density of Cu (111)@C system illustrated the charge enrichment on the carbon defects from Cu (Figure 5e), indicating the enhanced electron mobility and accelerated the charge transfer rate.38,39 Bader charge analysis suggests that about 2.4 electrons per supercell are transferred from Cu to C substrate (Figure S15 and Table S3), leading to the effective stability of *OCHO on charged carbon substrate.40 Therefore, carbon substrate can provide a synergistic effect to tune the surface electronic distributions and accelerate the charge transfer on catalyst surface to boost the enhanced HCOOH production.
19
Conclusions. In summary, we have demonstrated a novel and facile strategy to fabricate uniform Cu nanoparticles inlaid within porous carbon substrates via a mechanical ball-milling method. Impressively, the obtained Cu NPs-3@C catalyst
20
exhibited a high FEHCOOH of 78% at -1.0 V (RHE) with a selectivity of 87.6%, which outperformed top-level Cu-based catalysts. Moreover, the detailed DFT calculations illustrated that the obvious charge enrichment on the carbon surface leads to the enhanced adsorption of key *OCHO intermediates on Cu (111)@C system. The energy barrier of the rate-determining step has decreased from 0.42 eV on bare Cu (111) facet to 0.36 eV on Cu (111)@C system. This work provides a novel approach to prepare efficient and HCOOH-selective electrocatalyst and new insights into the carbon coating to steer the CO2RR performances.
